chunks.text: This is next-chapter, the public assembly repository, and the site you are listening on right now is the feature set: a library of three audiobooks about their own making, served as static files with no backend.
This chapter tours the site; later chapters cover its assembly, its prompt trail, and the machinery underneath. Start at the landing page, index dot h-t-m-l.

Its browser title reads "Next Chapter — a trilogy about its own making." The markup is nearly empty; a single inline call hands the player the whole library as data — three books: repo-story, landry-ui, and next-chapter itself. Every book credits the same artist, Brandon Landry.
Every chapter title carries a "Chapter N" prefix. Four chapters per book, each with a matching summary track. That three-book shape is the product of two scoping prompts.

The kernel is verbatim from the July twentieth foundation session, prompt twenty-eight: "the purpose of this project is to create the github page that is the interface to the audio books that talks about the repositories." It named landry-ui and repo-story, and fixed the site as a library of self-narrating books.

The third arrived the next day, prompt twenty-one of the July twenty-first vendored session: "I want to add one more repo, this one: next-chapter... which will complete the journey story of all of it." Two books became three.

The one-sentence description under each book answers a later trilogy-built prompt asking to "add a brief one short sentence that describes each book." The title phrase itself has no dictating prompt; it follows from that trilogy framing — an inference.

Next, the player — one paragraph, because it has its own book. It gives library view, chapter navigation with resume, playback speed, a time-synced transcript with follow and reading modes, and text-size control.
It is vanilla JavaScript, one global named RepoStoryPlayer, no build step: the landry-ui audiobook component, vendored rather than rebuilt.

The foundation session records the hesitation in prompt twenty-eight — "i am still conflicted about creating from scratch a reduced functionality user interface as opposed to reusing the landry ui" — and the resolution in prompt thirty-five: "reuse the landry ui, supersede adr 0002." Prompt forty-three locked the framing: the product is the player and the generator; the demonstration is their composition.

Now the feature built for the reviewer's clock: the Full and Summary toggle. Every chapter ships two tracks — the full narration, around seven minutes, and a summary, under two — with two buttons beside the transcript label to flip between them — the best-documented feature in the repository.
Its origin is verbatim, trilogy-built session, prompt eleven: "I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have...

add two buttons to the right of the TRANSCRIPT pane label: Full and Summary." The re-issued prompt added a text-first discipline — "Don't do anything yet except generate the summary and show it to me" — so the summary was reviewed as text before any interface or audio existed.
Prompt fifteen approved it and set the build order: "add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter." Two corrections followed.

Prompt sixteen moved the buttons "to appear after the word TRANSCRIPT." Prompt twenty-three caught the chapter pane still showing "the running length of the full length chapter" in summary mode; the fix threaded a computed summary clock through the whole time model.

Underneath, one durability detail. The read-along text lives in transcripts dot j-s-o-n, the merged timing data for every chapter. The page requests it with a version key: the first eight characters of the file's own content hash.

If the content changes, the key changes; if not, the browser keeps its copy. No prompt asks for this; it is the repo's standing durable-over-accurate rule — key on content, never on modification time — labeled inference.

One feature is present but inert: feedback dot j-s ships a styled control for flagging a transcription error, with logic to POST flags to a server. The published page never passes it a feedback URL, and there is no backend, so a flagged line is written to local storage and goes no further.

Partial by design: the backend was retired in decision record eight; the feature degrades quietly. Vendored code, no next-chapter prompt behind it. The site also installs and works offline, through a web manifest and a service worker in s-w dot j-s.
The worker precaches the shell files, caches each chapter's audio the first time it plays, and slices cached files into partial byte-range responses so seeking works offline.
Its cleanup list evicts two stale entries: a legacy single-file book, and one recalled bad-generation chapter, chapter one-zero-seven-three, replaced under the same name.

All of it is vendored, no next-chapter prompt behind it — inference — though an earlier war-game of the build plan attacked the worker's same-origin assumption, forcing the in-repo hosting that makes this caching viable at all. The newest feature is the quietest: the page counts its visitors.
The July thirtieth session opens by asking, quote, "is there a way to install google analytics here or something like that so I know who hits this page and when?" The answer was not Google.

The page carries a snippet for GoatCounter, a privacy-preserving hit counter: no cookies, no consent banner needed, recording only path, referrer, and a coarse browser and country — and its dashboard is public, open to anyone.
The assembler emits the snippet from an optional analytics key in trilogy dot j-s-o-n, so the site code has one source of truth and a build without that key ships no third-party script at all.

The same assembler prepends a cross-origin passthrough to the copied service worker, because the worker caches every response keyed by URL with no origin check, and the beacon's per-hit cache-buster would otherwise pile up quota-padded opaque cache entries.

The README discloses all of it, answering the follow-up prompt: "is there a note in the readme that mentions and links to this?"

In the browser tab, the favicon, favicon dot p-n-g, is the Next Chapter program mark.

Prompt thirty-one from the trilogy-built session reported it — "one small bug, no favicon" — and prompt thirty-two corrected the first fix: "use the favicon from their site, not my old wbt icon," pointing at nextchapterproject dot org. A registry key tells the assembler to copy it into place.

Last, the trail a reviewer can audit: provenance dot m-d and sources dot m-d. The first is auto-generated and records where the player was copied from, pinning a commit only when it can stand behind one.

The second is hand-written and pins each book's source — including the rule that this third book is narrated only through a pinned commit, because, per decision record nine, a book cannot contain its own generation.

The exact hash is an artifact of when the build ran; the pinned-range principle is verbatim. The whole layer answers foundation prompt twenty-seven, which asked what mechanism gives the reviewer "an unambiguous breadcrumb trail to follow."

None of the docs folder is written by hand.
A script assembles every file. That script is the next chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This is next-chapter, the public assembly repository, and the static site you are listening on is the artifact this chapter tours.

The landing page, index dot h-t-m-l, inlines the whole library: three books — repo-story, landry-ui, and next-chapter — every one credited to Brandon Landry, four chapters per book, each with a summary track.
That shape came from two prompts: a two-book kernel in the July twentieth foundation session and a trilogy addition the next day, recorded as decision record nine.

The player is the vendored landry-ui vanilla component — chapter navigation, resume, playback speed, time-synced transcripts with follow and reading modes, text sizing — a reuse decided live across three foundation-session prompts.

The Full and Summary toggle is the reviewer's time-budget feature, summaries under two minutes against chapters around seven, driven by the repo's best-documented prompt chain, from origin through two corrections.

Around them: a transcripts file cache-keyed on its own content hash rather than modification time; a feedback flag that is present but inert, saving only to local storage; an installable offline service worker with byte-range slicing and legacy eviction; privacy-preserving hit counting through GoatCounter, emitted from one registry key, disclosed in the README, with a cross-origin passthrough patched into the service worker; a favicon fixed by a two-prompt exchange; and provenance documents recording each book's source, pinning a commit only when they can stand behind one.
The toggle, favicon, and analytics carry verbatim prompts; the service worker, feedback, and cache key are vendored, stated as inference.

chunks.text: Chapter two. The player from chapter one plays whatever a registry hands it; this chapter is how the published site, the docs directory, gets built from three separate pipeline runs. Start with the registry: scripts slash trilogy dot json.

A small configuration file, and the whole plan for the site in data form. It carries a title — "Next Chapter, a trilogy about its own making" — a favicon key, and three books, each naming a slug, manifest path, transcripts path, and one-line description.
Those paths point into per-book run folders under repo-story, where the audio is gitignored but narration text and transcripts stay tracked and diffable.

No prompt dictates this file; it is where decisions made elsewhere — which three books, the site's title, the favicon — get recorded as config for the assembler to read. Next, the assembler: scripts slash build dash trilogy dash site.
It reads the registry and, for each book, converts the chapters manifest into the player's book structure with a function named book from manifest — and here is the design choice worth naming.

It does not reimplement that conversion; it imports the function from build underscore site dot py in the repo-story tree, the same code the pipeline itself uses to build a single book. One source of truth, derived from rather than copied, so the two can never drift.
That is the standing "durable over accurate" rule applied: no prompt says reuse this function, the rule says it.

It then copies each book's audio into docs slash audio slash the slug: every chapter file and any summary file — but only when the destination is missing or a different size on disk, so rebuilds skip unchanged audio.
Then it prunes: any file in the destination the new manifest does not expect gets reported as removing stale, and unlinked.

Only after the copy — which needs the plain names to find its source files — does it prefix every filename with the slug, so a book's first chapter becomes its slug, then slash, then chapter underscore zero zero zero one, keeping three books from colliding in one flat player.

The transcripts from all three books merge into a single transcripts dot json, and its cache-busting URL comes from the content itself: a sha256 hash of the merged bytes, first eight hex characters, as a version query string.
Change the content, the key changes; unchanged content keeps the browser's cache. A content hash, not a timestamp.

Then it copies the player's own files — player dot js, player dot css, the service worker, and the rest — plus the icons folder if present, and generates index dot html with all three books inlined into the player's init call.
This generator writes no feedback URL — which is why, as chapter one noted, the live feedback panel is inert. Two additions from July thirtieth: first, the registry gains an optional analytics key.

When it names a site code for goatcounter, a privacy-preserving hit counter, the assembler derives the endpoint and emits one script tag into the page head; when the key is absent, the page carries no third-party script at all — the site code lives in the registry, nowhere else.
The second addition guards the service worker.

The player's worker caches every response it fetches, keyed by URL, with no origin check, and the analytics beacon carries a per-hit cache-buster — every pageview would mint a new opaque cache entry, which browsers pad to a fixed multi-megabyte size against the origin's storage quota — unbounded growth crowding out the cached audio.
So the assembler patches the copied service worker on its way into docs, prepending a passthrough that catches cross-origin requests before the caching handler sees them.

Prepending rather than editing the upstream handler survives player-component drift; a marker makes the patch idempotent, so rebuilds never stack the guard. The tests assert the derived endpoint, the guard applied exactly once, and an opted-out build with no analytics.
Now the provenance rule, the sharp one. The player component is a copy of an external UI project, landry dash u i.

When the assembler records where the player came from, it shells out to git, reads the origin remote and the repository's top-level name, and pins an exact commit only if landry dash u i actually appears there — a genuine checkout of that project. Otherwise it writes a plain, unpinned description.
The in-code comment gives the reason: pinning that repository's HEAD would be, quote, provenance theater — a hash pointing at whatever repo encloses the directory is worse than no hash.
The result goes into docs slash PROVENANCE dot md, two honest lines: where the player was copied from, and that the audio and transcripts come from the run folders named in the registry.
The recap for the twenty-first records that this fix came from a research and QA pass, not a prompt — the assembler had been pinning the enclosing repo's HEAD. That fix is frozen into the tests.

The assembler ships with test underscore build underscore trilogy underscore site dot py, which exists because of one instruction from the twenty-first, the trilogy-built session, issued before any build code: "you see your directives to test first write code second right?" The test builds two fake books in a temporary directory, plants a fake player inside an unrelated git repository, and asserts the whole contract — filenames slug-prefixed, a summary file passing through, the registry's favicon replacing the player's default icon.

And the load-bearing negative one: the provenance string must contain no " at " marker — no pinned hash — precisely because the fake player sits in an unrelated repo, encoding the provenance-theater fix as a regression test. The test runs on the standard library alone.

One more piece, covered in full by book two but named here: the vendored generator. The repo-story tree inside this project, and its build script scripts slash vendor dash repo dash story, exist because of a decision from the twenty-first vendored session.
The prompt: "let's create this repo as a folder within next-chapter...

let's replay the commits excluding all personal info and unnecessary info you found." Rather than flip a private repository public, the owner had it replayed commit by commit into this repo, each snapshot scrubbed of excluded files and private text, each carrying a Replayed-From trailer back to its original.

The script refuses to run on main, and ships a verify mode that scans every replayed commit for banned tokens. That is the vendoring decision; book three tells how a leak was caught mid-flight. And nothing here deploys — the assembler assembles docs and stops.

Publishing is the owner's git push, a policy a PreToolUse hook enforces mechanically by blocking any agent push. The prompt from the twenty-first says it directly: do a final check for personal info, then, quote, give me the command to flip it public (the gh command), and i'll push it after that.

The assembler and registry themselves have no single authorizing prompt; they trace to an approved plan milestone and dated commits — that is inference, labeled as such. The same public-by-default stance applies to the prompts themselves — next.

summary_chunks.text: This chapter is the assembly: how three separate pipeline runs become the published site the player loads.

The registry, scripts slash trilogy dot json, is the plan in data form — a title, a favicon, an optional analytics key, and three books, each with slug, manifest, transcripts file, and description, pointing into pipeline run folders.
The assembler, scripts slash build dash trilogy dash site, reads that registry and converts each manifest with one function imported from the pipeline's own code rather than reimplemented.

It copies audio with a size-compare skip and stale-file pruning, prefixes filenames with each book's slug, merges all transcripts into one file cache-busted by the first eight characters of its content hash, and generates index dot html with the books inlined.

It emits an analytics tag only when the registry asks, and patches the copied service worker so cross-origin requests bypass its caching, else the analytics beacon's per-hit URLs would flood it with quota-padded opaque entries.

Its sharpest rule is provenance: it pins an exact commit for the player only when the player directory is a real checkout of the external landry-ui project — pinning any enclosing repo's HEAD would be, in the code's words, provenance theater.

That fix is frozen as a negative assertion in the test file, which exists because a prompt enforced test-first discipline. The vendored generator brought the pipeline in as scrubbed, replayed history. Nothing here deploys — the owner pushes, a hook enforces it — the stance the prompts get next.

chunks.text: This repo publishes not just the code but the prompts that made it. Every session's user prompts are exported verbatim and shipped alongside that session's recap, and a curated index, prompt-history.md, maps the whole set.

Every count those pages claim is re-derived from the export files themselves, so the numbers agree by construction, not by coincidence. The tool that produces the exports is a bash script named export-prompts.
Given a session name, it finds the newest Claude Code transcript for this repository and writes a companion file beside that session's recap in the vault. It keeps only what the human typed.
The extraction selects records of type user; if a message's content array contains a tool result, the whole message is dropped rather than risk leaking tool output.

Prefix filters then throw out anything that begins with a system-notification marker, a task-notification tag, a system-reminder tag, a local-command tag, or the line that opens a skill body. Empty prompts go too. One filter is newer than the rest.
The script also drops any transcript record flagged isMeta, the marker on user-role records the harness injected itself.

That flag closes a real gap: skill bodies loaded by the Skill tool carry no base-directory prefix line, so the older prefix filter missed them, and thousands of lines of skill text once landed in an export as if they were a prompt.

What the human typed is never flagged isMeta, so slash-command invocations survive in the trail. That fix landed on July thirtieth. Each surviving prompt then passes through inline redaction. The value is replaced but the line survives, so the prompt stays readable.

An email address becomes a redacted-email marker. Cookies, authorization headers, and CSRF tokens become redacted-credential. A private-key header and anything shaped like a known API token get markers of their own, and every home-directory path collapses to a tilde.

The finished file carries frontmatter typing it as prompts, a header noting the exclusions and the redaction, and each prompt numbered in sequence. After writing, if the leak scanner gitleaks is on the path, the script runs it over the file and warns, never blocks, on a hit.

All of this exists because of a single prompt from the July twentieth foundation session. It read, verbatim: "ok, this will be a public repo. add scanning verbage to the claude.md to ensure no private data leeks into commits.
Along with this I will want to be publishing the prompts alongside each session note that is captured with a slash vault recap." That one message seeds both the hygiene rules and the export pipeline.

The build order came a few prompts later, just as verbatim: "installed, build export-prompts and wire it in." The foundation recap records the result as the script plus eleven tests, written test-first, red to green. There is one more rule around the count, and it was earned rather than designed.

The project's CLAUDE.md says an implausibly low prompt count means the transcript format has drifted, so stop and investigate rather than publish a thin export. The rule exists because of a real miss.
On July twenty-first the counts were wrong: background task-notification blocks had been counted as prompts.

When the extractor learned to exclude those blocks, the foundation session's count fell from fifty-seven to forty-six, and the vendored session's rose from twenty-one to twenty-seven as other fixes landed. The exports were regenerated clean across the board.
The trigger was a sanity-check prompt from the same day's vendored session: "we are persisting the prompts, but not any of the responses.

do the requirements want us to preserve the responses from the AI also?" The old pre-fix recap line still shows the stale fifty-seven, left in place so the correction stays auditable. Next, the tests.

A script named test-export-prompts.sh runs the exporter against a tiny fixture transcript, one assertion for every rule the exporter enforces, gaining another whenever a new way of leaking non-prompt content turns up.

Two are load-bearing: a tool result planted in the fixture must not appear in the output, and a home path written as slash home slash testuser must be redacted to a tilde. The fixture also plants an email address so the test can confirm redaction fires.

That email is there because the public-repo wargame from the foundation session caught a real address in the author's own test fixture. The recap's phrasing was that fixtures are leak surface too; that finding is why the redaction assertions exist. The prompts do not ship raw and unindexed.

The README carries a Sessions and prompts table, one row per session, each linking the recap to its export with the prompt count beside it. The table traces to a July twenty-first instruction, verbatim: "ensure the links to prompts are on the readme. and include any links to resources there ...

so the reviewer can navigate easily." Behind it sits an earlier foundation prompt asking what mechanism gives the reviewer, quote, "an unambigous breadcrumb trail to follow of how I am building this." Above the raw exports sits prompt-history.md, the curated index, and beside it config-history.md, the decoder document whose command glossary must already define every slash command an export invokes before it publishes, so a reviewer never meets an unexplained command.

None of those pages is kept correct by hand. A gate named check-session-wrapup starts from the newest session named in the vault's Session Log and re-derives every published prompt count by counting prompts in the export files themselves, never by comparing one copied number against another.

It confirms the recap and the export exist and link each other, that the session's counts and a matching totals line appear in the README, the same in prompt-history.md, and that every slash command the new export uses has its entry in the glossary.
Any disagreement fails the gate, one line per problem. The gate exists because a July thirtieth recap shipped with prompt-history.md, the curated index, left un-updated.

The instruction that followed asked, verbatim, to "add them as checks to the wrap up process so they don't get missed again."

All of this is wrapped in hygiene.

Before every commit, the staged diff is scanned, by gitleaks or by grep, across three classes: credentials, identity, and machine internals. That rule traces to the same July twentieth public-repo prompt and to a follow-up asking to wargame the strategy for securing a public repo.
On top of it sits a private token-map scan for identifiers a regular expression cannot catch.

That second scan exists because of a July twenty-first lesson, told straight: quoted agent output inside prompt exports had leaked infrastructure identifiers and family names past gitleaks and into pushed history.
The prompt that met it was verbatim: "this is still private and we can force push to rewrite the remote history.

this does expose that we need to scan our prompts also as a source of private data leakage." The fix was a full-history rewrite while the repo was still private, and a new standing rule that checks every staged diff and every prompt export against a gitignored banned-token list.
Prompts are half the audit trail. The config they ran under is the other half, and that is the last chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This part of the repo is the prompt trail: the machinery that publishes not just the code but the prompts that made it. Its core is a bash script named export-prompts.

It finds the newest Claude Code transcript for the repository, keeps only what the human typed, and drops assistant replies, tool results, system notifications, skill-expansion blocks, and any record the harness flagged isMeta — the marker that catches injected skill bodies the older prefix filter missed.
Each surviving prompt is redacted inline, the value replaced but the line preserved: emails, credentials, private keys, token-shaped strings, and home paths each become a marker.

It writes one numbered file of verbatim prompts per session, linked to that session's recap, then runs the leak scanner gitleaks over what it wrote. A companion test script, test-export-prompts.sh, asserts those rules against a fixture transcript.
A plausibility rule, earned after task-notification blocks once inflated the counts, says an implausibly low count means transcript drift, so stop and investigate.

A gate named check-session-wrapup re-derives every published count from the export files themselves and fails when the Session Log, the README's table and totals, prompt-history.md, the curated index, or config-history.md's command glossary disagrees.

Wrapping it all is public-repo hygiene: a scan before every commit across credentials, identity, and machine internals, plus a private token-map scan for identifiers regex cannot see, added after quoted agent output leaked past gitleaks.
A July twentieth request to publish the prompts drove every piece.

chunks.text: This last chapter covers the parts of the repository that exist so its claims can be checked: the configuration the sessions ran under, and the memory that carried context between them, both made readable to a reviewer who was never at the keyboard. Start with the configuration.

Throughout the project the agent ran under machine-level config that lives outside the repo, on the owner's laptop: global conduct rules, session hooks, a handful of skills. Vault notes and prompt exports refer to those files constantly, and a reviewer reading a clone cannot see any of them.
The fix is a directory named dot-claude at the repo root holding actual copies. The whole feature comes from one prompt in the config-mirror session on July twentieth.
The owner noticed that paths and skill references pointed at his local filesystem and wrote, verbatim, that this hides things from the reviewer.

He asked for a local dot-claude folder whose contents mirror and duplicate the system files, but explicitly, so that a reviewer can see what I am running and can cross-reference paths they see in vault notes and other committed documents.

He closed with an instruction to do a complete repo scan, update docs as needed, and commit. Every design property of the feature follows from that wording, and the decision is recorded as architecture decision record seven.
Because the prompt asked for a copy a reviewer can trust, the mirror is generated, never hand-typed. The generator is scripts slash sync-claude-mirror.

It treats the global configuration as the single source of truth and derives the mirror from it: the orientation hook claude-orient and the push guard deny-git-push dot s h from the machine's bin directory, the global conduct file and settings, and four skills copied in full, conduct, vault, vet, and wargame.
The browser skill, gstack, is about one point seven gigabytes upstream, so only its entry points come through, on an allowlist.
The copy is rsync in archive mode, which preserves executable bits, with copy-links to resolve the skill symlinks that point into a dotfiles repo, and delete to prune anything stale.

All of the script's roots, where the global config sits, where bin sits, where the mirror goes, are environment variables with computed defaults, never hardcoded absolute paths; that is the repo's durable-over-accurate rule applied to its own tooling.
If any expected source is missing, the script exits with an error instead of writing a thin mirror, because a silently incomplete copy would misrepresent the setup.

And a check mode dry-runs the sync and reports drift without writing anything; the project runs it as a gate before committing any change that touches configuration. None of those durability properties appear in the prompt.
They are the standing rule, an inference about how trustworthy gets implemented, not a quoted instruction. Not everything in the folder is inert. A companion README draws the line.

The in-tree settings file and the in-tree skills genuinely load here, and the push guard runs from the copy inside dot-claude, so the rule that the agent never pushes is enforced by readable code that travels with every clone.

The files suffixed dot-global are documentation only, deliberately unregistered, because the machine's global hooks already fire; loading the copies too would double-fire them, orientation twice per session, the brevity rule twice per prompt.
The mirror script has tests, and no prompt asked for them; they exist because of the project's standing rule, tests first, code second.

The suite, test-sync-claude-mirror dot s h, builds a fake global, bin, and skills tree in a temporary directory through those same environment overrides, so it never touches the real machine config or the repo's own mirror. It runs six phases.

Two of its teeth: one edits a source file and confirms check mode flags the drift, then that a resync clears it; another deletes a source file and confirms the sync fails loudly rather than producing a thin copy.
The others verify that executable bits survive, symlinks resolve, stale mirror files get pruned, and the hand-written README and settings are left alone. Next, memory.

At the start of every session a hook, session-start dot s h, prints exactly three pointer lines into the agent's context: the latest recap, the count of open todos, the count of open probes. Pointers, never bodies; enough to orient, then read deeper on demand.

It anchors itself to this repo's vault explicitly and delegates every read to scripts slash vault-digest, a plain grep-and-awk reader with subcommands for summaries, notes by type or by concern, the latest recap, todos, probes, backlinks, and full-text search.
A design note dated June twenty-ninth, before this project began, records why it is built that way: dropping the Obsidian-app dependency made memory work headless and across parallel sessions.

The repo inherits that machinery rather than authoring it; the foundation session's conduct-init command stamped the local copies in one stroke, and the mirror is what lets a reviewer read the actual scripts.

The memory itself lives in the vault directory, a real in-tree folder of Obsidian-compatible markdown. It holds the session records as recap-and-prompts pairs, each recap beside the exported prompts that drove it, plus todos, project notes, a vet, and the architecture decision records with an index.
The instruction to keep those records is verbatim from the foundation session on July twentieth: let's start collecting A-D-Rs.

Some are superseded, an S3 audio plan, an early plan to build a minimal player from scratch, and they are kept on purpose; others were never replaced at all, a Lambda ingestion path deferred to a later version, the two-books plan extended into the trilogy.

The owner audited exactly that choice in the vendored session on July twenty-first, granting that in normal development superseded records are not removed, but asking for an audit for the sake of making the repo uncluttered, because the reviewer will not look at things that are hard to find or hidden behind clutter.
The resolution keeps the superseded records under clear supersession banners with an index marking active versus retired, because the audiobooks narrate how the decisions evolved.

And the policy stayed live to the day this chapter was recorded: on July thirtieth the pipeline narrating this book rewrote its own model split, the decision Fable plans, Opus executes giving way to Fable writes, Opus researches, because a newer model generation made Opus the stronger reasoner and Fable the stronger writer of English, while the enforcement, model pins in settings and in each agent's frontmatter, never moved.
A model-to-task mapping is a dated decision, not a permanent one. That closes the book.

The published site, the assembler that builds it, the prompt trail behind every feature, and this mirror of the configuration it all ran under: the whole build is auditable end to end, which was the point from the first prompt to the last.

summary_chunks.text: The closing chapter covers the configuration and the memory the sessions ran under, both made readable to a reviewer who was never at the keyboard.

The centerpiece is the in-tree dot-claude mirror: checked-in copies of the machine-level config the agent actually ran, so paths cited in vault notes and prompt exports resolve to real files in the clone.

The script scripts slash sync-claude-mirror generates it from the global config, the single source of truth: the orientation hook, the push-guard script, the global conduct file and settings, four skills in full, and the large gstack browser skill allowlisted to entry points only.

Its roots are environment-derived, it fails loudly on a missing source, and a check mode gates every config commit against drift. The in-tree settings and skills are live, the push guard included; files suffixed dot-global are documentation only, unregistered so the global hooks do not double-fire.

A tests-first suite exercises the script against a fake global directory in six phases. For memory, a session-start hook prints three pointer lines, latest recap, open todos, open probes, and delegates reading to vault-digest, a headless grep-and-awk tool.

The vault holds session recap-and-prompt pairs, todos, projects, a vet, and architecture decision records, superseded ones kept on purpose after a legibility audit; the pipeline's own model-split decision was superseded the day this chapter was recorded.
One verbatim prompt from the July twentieth config-mirror session drives the whole mirror. With that, the build is auditable end to end.
